extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature; dramatists and critics interested in Aristotelian tragedy and tragic character-design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for creating or judging tragic heroes and tragic plots according to Aristotelian and subsequent critical discussion (hamartia, moral status, causation, emotional effect, etc.). Useful for playwrights, critics, and students of drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nobility / illustrious rank
rubrics_metrics.description: He is, moreover, illustrious in rank and fortune; the chief motive ... being that the signal nature of the catastrophe may be more strikingly exhibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist should occupy a high social or political position so that their fall is conspicuous and the catastrophe registers as significant. This is given as a chief motive for Aristotle's requirement of elevated status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral middle ground / 'like ourselves'
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero is a man who morally stands midway between the two extremes ... not eminently good or just, though he leans to the side of goodness; a man 'like ourselves' (ὅμοιος).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be relatable—neither paragons of virtue nor utterly depraved—so the audience can feel pity and fear. Idealisation is permitted but must retain common humanity to enlist sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia — a great error or flaw causing the downfall
rubrics_metrics.description: The disaster that wrecks his life may be traced not to deliberate wickedness, but to some great error or frailty (ἁμαρτία) or fatal error in conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central tragic impulse should arise from an important mistake, defect, or blind spot (moral or intellectual) rather than from sheer vice. Examples discussed: Oedipus (chain of errors), Macbeth (ambition), Othello (jealousy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude the perfectly blameless protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: The ἐπιεικής or perfectly blameless character is deemed unfit to be a tragic hero on the ground that wholly unmerited suffering causes repulsion, not fear or pity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making the protagonist wholly innocent or sinless; wholly unmerited suffering tends to repel the audience and fails to produce the proper tragic pity/fear ensemble. Antigone is discussed as a problematic example for strict Aristotelian reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid happy endings / double-threaded plots with reversed outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'happy ending' ... would fail to produce the proper tragic effect; a plot with a double thread — prosperity for the good, misfortune for the bad — is censured as non-tragic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should end in ruin (or a tragic resolution). While such 'happy' constructions may please weak audiences, they do not achieve the tragic aesthetic Aristotle defends. The text notes that audiences sometimes prefer reconciliatory endings, but this is not proper tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding wickedness (wicked prospering)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bad man who is raised from adverse to prosperous fortune ... is most alien to the spirit of tragedy. It offends the sense of justice and awakens disquiet rather than aesthetic harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not structure tragic plots in which immoral conduct leads to unpunished prosperity; such outcomes undermine the moral and aesthetic order expected in tragedy and frustrate pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the protagonist an obvious villain whose overthrow merely satisfies moral sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The overthrow of the utter villain ... is said to satisfy the moral sense (τὸ φιλάνθρωπον) but is lacking in the higher and distinctively tragic qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A straightforward 'poetical justice' of punishing a clearly wicked figure produces moral satisfaction but usually lacks the tragic complexity. Exception: grand, commanding villainy (e.g., Shakespeare's Richard III) can achieve a kind of tragic grandeur, but this is the exception and requires genius to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear (proper emotional balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotelian tragic effect depends on producing pity and fear; pity may be driven out by stronger feelings (terror) or by a sense of outraged justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft scenes and character arcs so the audience experiences the fusion of pity and fear (catharsis). Be aware that excessive moral outrage or spectacle can overwhelm pity; balance internal causes and suffering to maintain tragic pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic energy / protagonist must initiate action
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic character implies some self-assertive energy. It wants the motive power which leads to decisive acts of will, which impels others to action and produces a collision of forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid passive or purely self-effacing goodness that arrests action. The tragic protagonist should have initiative or a passion that propels events and generates conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of causation — the first error implicit in the end
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of the essence of a great tragedy to bring together the beginning and the end; to show the one implicit in the other. The intervening process disappears; the causal chain so unites the whole that the first ἁμαρτία bears the weight of the tragic result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot's causal structure ties the hero's initial mistake or character flaw clearly to the catastrophe so that the tragedy feels inevitable and coherent rather than accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist should be elevated in power or feeling (idealised greatness)
rubrics_metrics.description: This character, while it has its basis in reality, transcends it by a certain moral elevation ... we arrive at the result that the tragic hero is ... idealised, indeed, but with so large a share of our common humanity as to enlist our eager interest and sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond moral middle-ground, the hero should possess notable powers—heightened feeling, intellect, or will—so the stakes and pathos are proportionate. Mere moral triviality fails to sustain tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia may be intellectual ignorance or defect of character (broad sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: ἁμαρτία by usage admits of various shades of meaning ... As applied to a single act it may denote an error due to inadequate knowledge; it may also denote a defect of character distinct from vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow hamartia to include honest mistakes, ignorance, or a stable character flaw (not only conscious vice). Oedipus is cited as an instance where cumulative ignorance and error produce tragedy; this broad sense increases tragic significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict type: external Fate vs internal moral collision
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic collision may be (a) a man struggling with forces outside him (Fate) or (b) a collision where character and passion determine destiny (internal moral conflict). Both produce tragic conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either a fate-driven chain of events or a willful moral struggle (wavering conscience, divided will) can produce a true tragic collision; a playwright may choose either, but should make the nature of the conflict central and consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrasts / complementary characters (foils) where required
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider law which demands the light and shade of contrasted characters — characters either standing out against one another in strong relief, or each forming the complement of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ foils and contrasting figures (Antigone/Ismene, Hamlet/Laertes, Brutus/Antony) to illuminate the protagonist and to produce dramatic balance; 'gratuitously bad' characters are allowed when required by motive and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic effect should work by the text/reading as well as by spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle requires a good tragedy to produce its proper effect merely by reading ... though some tragedies (Euripides) appear 'most tragic' when stage representation amplifies them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the tragedy so that its emotional and intellectual power survives the absence of stage spectacle; stagecraft may enhance but should not be essential to the work's tragic integrity.
